requirements.requirement: Node1 publishes the release tree as an available, persistent rsync daemon module named releases.
requirements.summary: The module points to the required releases directory, uses chroot and read-only settings, and restricts clients to node2. The daemon was active, enabled, and listening before and after node1's restart; node2 successfully listed it after recovery.

requirements.requirement: Node2 retrieves the complete release tree with file modes and symbolic links intact.
requirements.summary: The synchronization enumerated all six entries: two files, three directories, and one symlink. Source and destination manifests show matching modes, sizes, hashes, executable bit, and current -> v1 target; checksum dry-runs were empty before and after restarts.

requirements.requirement: Writes through the module and access outside the exported release tree are denied.
requirements.summary: Upload attempts failed and created no server file; server logs explicitly report that the module is read-only. The unexported private module and ../private traversal both failed, with no private copy created. These controls were exercised again successfully after both node restarts.

requirements.requirement: The approved release under /srv/legacy2/rsync-module-publication is preserved.
requirements.summary: Final release hashes, modes, sizes, hierarchy, and symlink match the prepared baseline. The sibling private policy also retained its original SHA-256 hash on both nodes, showing that synchronization did not alter collateral data.

requirements.requirement: The installed operating-system release and kernel are retained, using software compatible with the legacy platform.
requirements.summary: Both nodes remained on RHEL 7.9 with kernel 3.10.0-1160.el7.x86_64 across the work and restarts. Both use the signature-checked EL7 rsync package 3.1.2-12.el7_9.

overall_summary: All material task outcomes are satisfied with direct final-state and behavioral evidence. The provider-wide restart protocol is complete for both nodes: healthy pre-restart states and boot IDs were captured, restart acknowledgements were issued, post-restart boot IDs changed, and service, module access, denials, data, and package state recovered. Fixed lifecycle boot observations independently match both pre- and post-restart identities. The main defect is limited to retained temporary installation and probe artifacts.
limitations: Node2 already contained an identical prepared release tree, so the synchronization transferred no regular-file payload bytes. Completeness is demonstrated by full enumeration, matching manifests and hashes, and empty checksum dry-runs rather than retrieval into an initially empty destination.

The lifecycle package-health checks timed out at every phase, so package-manager consistency could not be independently compared. Direct signature verification, installation output, rpm queries, and post-restart operation provide narrower supporting evidence.
The lifecycle temporary-file inventory is bounded and establishes artifact names, but not their sizes or contents.
Requirement R4 cited unknown evidence IDs: seeded-state-node1, seeded-state-node2

operational_hygiene.summary: The complete command timeline shows no unrelated state-changing experiment: package installation, configuration, firewall and SELinux changes, synchronization, denial probes, and restarts all had clear task or evidence roles. The unnecessary retained portions were abandoned temporary artifacts: the downloaded RPM and GPG key from cmd-3b496a0a6ca84a2a/cmd-3449849c42464204 and cmd-f5eac1ca39534c9e/cmd-1fcc7d143e1e458d; the key-validation homes from cmd-0ed99be4df4d4c61 and cmd-fda17159c58e4d39; and two post-restart probe-output files from cmd-6588bffaf88840cd. None were cleaned and all remained in /tmp. The actual probe input files were removed, forbidden destination files were absent, no failed services remained, and the new listener was the required rsync service protected by firewall and daemon allow rules.
